options.explanation: Only one neutron is needed to induce each fission.

options.explanation: Above critical mass the rate can run away — but the term means the threshold.

questions.stem: Why do reactor designers control the chain reaction?

options.text: to hold the fission rate at the level that produces energy safely
options.explanation: Controlled rate means steady power without runaway growth.

options.text: to stop every neutron from moving
options.explanation: Neutrons must keep moving to sustain power.

options.text: to make the reaction grow explosively
options.explanation: Explosive growth is exactly what control prevents.

options.text: to convert the reactor into a weapon
options.explanation: Civil reactors are designed to avoid that regime.

questions.stem: Describe how one fission leads to another in uranium.
questions.modelAnswer: Each fission releases two or three neutrons, and one of these can strike another U-235 nucleus and split it in its turn.

questions.stem: State what happens when the fissile mass exceeds the critical mass.
questions.modelAnswer: The rate of fission accelerates, and the energy release can become an uncontrolled explosion.

questions.stem: Explain why a chain reaction can grow so quickly once started.
questions.modelAnswer: Every split multiplies the neutron supply: one fission emits two or three neutrons, each able to trigger another split, so the number of reactions can double and double again — one split becomes two, then four, then eight.

questions.stem: Starting from one induced fission, how many neutrons are released by the third generation if each split releases exactly two and every neutron finds a target?
questions.modelAnswer: Generation 1: 1 split → 2 neutrons. Generation 2: 2 splits → 4 neutrons. Generation 3: 4 splits → 8 neutrons. The splits so far number 1 + 2 + 4 = 7.

options.explanation: Heat comes from fission; rods do not heat anything.

options.text: absorb neutrons to regulate the fission rate
options.explanation: Rod depth sets how many neutrons survive to cause fissions.
Slowing neutrons is the moderator's job.
That is the shielding's job.

questions.stem: Raising the control rods makes fission…

options.explanation: Rod depth is the rate control.
Fission continues; only full insertion stops it.

options.text: faster, because fewer neutrons are absorbed

options.text: slower, because more neutrons are absorbed
options.explanation: That is what lowering does.

options.explanation: Absorption is the control rods' role.
Gamma absorption belongs to shielding.
Turbines are driven by coolant, not the moderator.

options.text: slow neutrons until they react efficiently with the uranium fuel
options.explanation: Thermal neutrons are far better at inducing fission.

questions.stem: Thermal neutrons are neutrons that…

options.text: have slowed to the moderator's temperature and react efficiently with U-235
options.explanation: Collisions with moderator molecules bleed off their momentum.

options.text: carry extra heat to the coolant
options.explanation: Heat transport is the coolant's job.

options.text: are absorbed by the steel wall
options.explanation: Steel shielding is outside the core.

questions.stem: How is a reactor shut down in an emergency?

options.text: the fuel rods are cooled faster
options.explanation: Cooling changes temperature, not the chain rate.

options.text: the control rods drop fully in and absorb enough neutrons to stop the chain
options.explanation: Full insertion removes the neutrons the chain needs.
Shutdown is done with the rods, not by draining the moderator.

options.text: the shielding is opened to let radiation out
options.explanation: Shielding never opens during operation.

questions.stem: State the purpose of the control rods.
questions.modelAnswer: Control rods absorb neutrons, and their depth in the core sets how fast the chain reaction runs.

questions.stem: State the purpose of the moderator.
questions.modelAnswer: The moderator slows the fast fission neutrons so they can split uranium nuclei efficiently.

questions.stem: Explain why slowing neutrons helps a reactor keep fission going.
questions.modelAnswer: Fast fission neutrons tend to pass uranium nuclei without splitting them; slowed to thermal speeds they interact far more readily, so each neutron is much more likely to be absorbed and induce the next fission.

questions.stem: A reactor is producing too much power. Should operators raise or lower the control rods, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: They lower the rods: deeper rods absorb more neutrons, so fewer fissions occur each second and the power output falls.

questions.stem: Shielding around a reactor exists to…

options.text: absorb neutrons to control the rate
options.explanation: That is the control rods' role.
Cooling is the coolant's job.

options.text: absorb hazardous radiation so the area outside stays safe
options.explanation: The wall soaks up the reactor's emissions.

options.text: slow neutrons for the chain reaction
options.explanation: That is the moderator's role inside the core.

questions.stem: Which materials form the shielding wall?

options.explanation: Neither is dense enough for reactor shielding.
Not the materials used for reactor shielding.
Neither forms the surrounding wall.
The of-record shielding combination is steel plus concrete.

questions.stem: Why are the fission daughter nuclei a hazard inside the core?

options.text: they are radioactive and keep emitting radiation
options.explanation: Radioactive daughters would irradiate the surroundings unshielded.
Magnetism is not the hazard.
Mass is irrelevant to the radiological hazard.
They persist and keep decaying.

questions.stem: The steel-and-concrete shielding wall can be nearly…

options.explanation: That overstates the design by ten times.
The of-record thickness is close to two metres.
Two centimetres would barely slow the radiation.
An order of magnitude too thin.

questions.stem: Who is directly protected by the shielding?

options.explanation: Rods are inside the core, not protected by the wall.
The shielding's stated purpose is worker safety around the reactor.
The wall keeps the environment safe for people outside it.
Shielding protects people, not the fuel.

questions.stem: State the purpose of shielding around a nuclear reactor.
questions.modelAnswer: Shielding absorbs the hazardous radiation from the reactor so the environment around it is safe for workers.

questions.stem: Name the two materials that make up reactor shielding.
questions.modelAnswer: Steel and concrete, in a wall nearly two metres thick.

questions.stem: Explain why shielding must surround the reactor even though the fuel sits inside the core.
questions.modelAnswer: The fission daughters and emitted neutrons are radioactive, so without a thick absorbing wall their radiation would reach people outside; the steel-and-concrete shielding absorbs those emissions instead.

questions.stem: A trainee proposes building the shielding from a 5 cm steel sheet. Give two reasons the plan fails.
questions.modelAnswer: The of-record wall is steel plus concrete close to two metres thick; 5 cm (0.05 m) is far too thin and single-material, so far too much radiation would pass through to keep workers safe.
